title: The national grid — getting electricity from power station to your home
examTip: High voltage → low current → less power lost as heat in cables (P_lost = I²R). This is WHY the grid uses high voltage. Don't just say 'to save energy'. You need to explain the physics.
introTips: The national grid uses very high voltages, up to 400,000 V. This cuts the energy wasted in cables.
Transformers only work with AC (alternating current). This is why mains electricity is AC.
The transformer equation is V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. The voltage ratio equals the turns ratio.
intro: When you plug something in, the electricity may have been made hundreds of miles away. It could come from a wind farm off Scotland or a nuclear power station in Somerset. It could come from a gas plant in Yorkshire. Getting it to you without wasting most of it is a tricky engineering problem. The answer is to use very high voltages to send it a long way. Then the voltage is stepped back down before it reaches your kettle. This is one of the cleverest uses of physics in everyday life.

keyPoints.heading: How the national grid works
keyPoints.content: The national grid is the network of cables and transformers that carries electricity across the UK. It runs from power stations to homes, schools and businesses. Electricity is generated at power stations at around 25,000 V (25 kV). A step-up transformer then raises this to up to 400,000 V (400 kV). This is for sending it a long way through high-voltage overhead cables. At the other end, a series of step-down transformers lower the voltage in stages: - 400 kV down to 33 kV for heavy industry - 11 kV for lighter industry - finally 230 V for homes Why use such high voltages? Start from P = IV. Say the power (P) is fixed and the voltage (V) is very high. Then the current (I) must be very low. Then use P_lost = I²R. A lower current means far less power wasted as heat in the resistance of the cables. Doubling the voltage halves the current. Power loss ∝ I², so this cuts cable losses by four times.
writeBullets: National grid — the network of cables and transformers carrying electricity across the UK
Generated at ~25 kV → stepped up to ~400 kV to send it a long way
Stepped down to 230 V for homes by a series of step-down transformers
High voltage → low current (P = IV, fixed P). I = P/V, so higher V means lower I
Low current → less power wasted as heat in cables: P_lost = I²R (power loss ∝ I²)

keyTerms.def: The network of cables and transformers that distributes electricity from power stations to consumers across the UK
Power (W) = current (A) × voltage (V); at constant power, higher V means lower I
Power wasted as heat in cables = current squared × resistance; lower current dramatically reduces heat loss

keyPoints.memTip: High V → low I → low I²R loss. The grid uses high voltage because cutting the current cuts cable losses by its square.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The I²R equation is the key to explaining WHY high voltage is used. Go beyond 'less energy is wasted'. Show why a lower current reduces heating losses.

keyPoints.heading: Transformers — how they work
keyPoints.content: Transformers only work with alternating current (AC). An AC current in the primary coil makes a changing magnetic field. That changing field induces a voltage in the secondary coil. DC makes a constant magnetic field, which does not induce a voltage. A step-up transformer has more turns on the secondary than the primary. It increases voltage and decreases current. A step-down transformer has fewer turns on the secondary. It decreases voltage and increases current. The transformer equation: V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. That is, primary voltage ÷ secondary voltage = primary turns ÷ secondary turns. For an ideal (100% efficient) transformer: V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ (power in = power out). Worked example: a transformer has 200 turns on the primary and 2000 on the secondary. The input voltage is 230 V. Output voltage = 230 × (2000 ÷ 200) = 2300 V (step-up, ratio 1:10).
writeBullets: Transformers only work with AC. A changing current makes a changing magnetic field, which induces a voltage
Step-up transformer — more turns on the secondary. Increases voltage, decreases current
Step-down transformer — fewer turns on the secondary. Decreases voltage, increases current
Transformer equation: V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂ (voltage ratio = turns ratio)
Ideal transformer: V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ (power in = power out, assuming 100% efficiency)

keyTerms.def: A transformer with more turns on the secondary coil than the primary — increases voltage, decreases current
A transformer with fewer turns on the secondary than the primary — decreases voltage, increases current
The transformer equation: ratio of voltages equals ratio of turns on each coil
For an ideal transformer, power input = power output (100% efficient)

keyPoints.memTip: Step UP = more turns on secondary → V goes up, I goes down. Step DOWN = fewer turns → V goes down, I goes up.
keyPoints.tutor_note: A common exam question asks you to find missing values using V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. Then you use V₁I₁ = V₂I₂ to find the secondary current. Practise both steps together.

keyPoints.heading: Generating electricity
keyPoints.content: Most traditional power stations work in a chain: - burn fuel (coal, gas, oil), or use nuclear fission (uranium), to release heat - the heat boils water to make steam - the steam drives a turbine - the turbine drives a generator - the generator makes electricity by electromagnetic induction (spinning a coil inside a magnetic field) Renewable options: - wind turbines: wind pushes the blades → turbine → generator. No steam is needed - hydroelectric: flowing water drives turbines. Very reliable - solar photovoltaic: light makes electricity directly in semiconductor cells. No turbine at all Note: nuclear power still uses the steam-turbine-generator chain, just like fossil fuels. But it makes no CO₂ while generating. The key difference is between PV solar (no turbine) and everything else (turbine needed).
writeBullets: Traditional chain: fuel or fission → heat → steam → turbine → generator → electricity
Electromagnetic induction — electricity made by spinning a coil in a magnetic field
Wind turbine — wind turns the blades directly and drives a generator (no steam)
Hydroelectric — flowing water drives a turbine, which drives a generator (no steam)
Solar PV — light is turned directly into electricity. No turbine, no steam, no generator
Nuclear — the same steam-turbine-generator chain as fossil fuels. No CO₂, but radioactive waste

keyTerms.def: The process of generating a voltage (and current) by moving a conductor through a magnetic field — how generators work
A device with blades that spin when hit by steam, water, or wind — drives a generator to produce electricity
Technology that directly converts light energy to electrical energy using semiconductor cells — no turbine needed

keyPoints.memTip: MOST energy sources: heat → steam → turbine → generator. Solar PV is the odd one out. It goes straight to electricity.
keyPoints.tutor_note: It is easy to forget that nuclear power still uses turbines and steam. It is not really different from coal. It just has a different heat source.

keyPoints.heading: Energy sources and the environment
keyPoints.content: The UK uses a mix of energy sources. This balances reliability, cost and harm to the environment. Non-renewables: - Coal: the most CO₂ per kWh and the cheapest to burn. It is being phased out. - natural gas: less CO₂ than coal. It is flexible, and can be turned on quickly to meet peak demand. - nuclear: no CO₂ while generating, and a reliable baseload. But it makes radioactive waste and costs a lot to build. Renewables: - Solar PV: no emissions, quick to install and cheap at scale. But it is intermittent, and only works when it is sunny. - wind: no emissions, and the cheapest new electricity source in the UK by the 2020s. But it is intermittent. - hydroelectric: reliable, controllable and no emissions. But it needs rivers and dams, and affects ecosystems. - tidal: very predictable, because tides never stop. But it is expensive to build. - biomass: burns plant material. It may be carbon-neutral if crops regrow, but this is debated. UK energy mix (approximate 2023): ~40% renewables (mainly offshore wind), ~40% gas, ~15% nuclear, and the rest other. The grid needs baseload power (constant and reliable, like nuclear). It needs a peak load response (flexible, like gas). It also needs a growing share of renewables, with energy storage.
writeBullets: Non-renewable — fossil fuels (coal, gas, oil) + nuclear. Finite supply. Coal has the most CO₂
Coal — high CO₂, cheapest to burn, being phased out in the UK
Natural gas — less CO₂ than coal. Flexible response to peak load
Nuclear — no CO₂ while generating, reliable baseload. Makes radioactive waste
Solar and wind — zero emissions, now the cheapest new electricity. But intermittent (depends on weather)
Hydroelectric — reliable, controllable, no emissions. Needs rivers and dams (affects ecosystems)
Tidal — predictable and reliable. Expensive to build and maintain
Biomass — burns plant material. May be carbon-neutral. How sustainable it is is debated

keyTerms.def: Energy source that is naturally replenished and will not run out — wind, solar, hydro, tidal, biomass
Energy source that will run out — fossil fuels (coal, gas, oil) and nuclear (uranium)
Not always available — solar only works when sunny, wind only when it blows
The constant minimum level of electricity demand — met by reliable sources like nuclear and hydroelectric

keyPoints.memTip: Renewables are FREE to run but INTERMITTENT. Non-renewables are RELIABLE but produce CO₂ (or waste).
keyPoints.tutor_note: 6-mark questions often ask you to evaluate energy sources. Give both advantages AND disadvantages. Consider reliability, cost and harm to the environment.

1.question: A transformer has 500 turns on the primary coil and 5000 turns on the secondary. The input voltage is 230 V. What is the output voltage?
1.correctFeedback: Correct! V₂ = V₁ × (n₂/n₁) = 230 × (5000/500) = 230 × 10 = 2300 V. This is a step-up transformer (ratio 1:10).
1.wrongFeedback: Use V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. Rearrange: V₂ = V₁ × (n₂/n₁) = 230 × (5000 ÷ 500) = 230 × 10 = 2300 V. More turns on the secondary → higher voltage (step-up).

0.question: Why does the national grid transmit electricity at very high voltages (up to 400,000 V)?
options: High voltage means lower current. This greatly reduces the power wasted as heat in the cables (P_lost = I²R)
High voltage makes the electricity travel faster through the cables
High voltage stops the cables overheating from solar radiation
High voltage is safer for the engineers who maintain the cables
0.correctFeedback: Exactly right! At constant power, higher voltage means lower current (from P = IV). Lower current hugely reduces heating losses in the cables. This is because P_lost = I²R, so loss is proportional to current squared.
0.wrongFeedback: The answer is about cutting energy waste in the cables. From P = IV: higher V → lower I. From P_lost = I²R: lower I → much less power wasted as heat. That is why the grid uses high voltages. It is not for speed, and not for safety.

3.question: Which energy source can generate electricity without using a turbine?
3.correctFeedback: Correct! Solar PV turns light directly into electricity using semiconductor cells. No turbine, no steam, no generator. All the others (including nuclear and wind) drive a generator with a turbine.
3.wrongFeedback: Solar PV is the only common source that turns light directly into electricity without a turbine. Nuclear, wind and hydroelectric all use turbines connected to generators.

commonMistakes: Saying the grid uses high voltage 'to save energy' without explaining how. Link it to P = IV (lower current) and P_lost = I²R (lower heating losses).
Thinking transformers work with DC. They only work with AC. DC makes a constant, unchanging magnetic field. That does not induce a voltage in the secondary coil.
Mixing up step-up and step-down transformers. Step-up has MORE turns on the secondary (voltage goes UP). Step-down has FEWER turns on the secondary (voltage goes DOWN).
Forgetting that nuclear power stations still use turbines and steam. The difference from fossil fuels is the heat source (fission, not burning), not how electricity is generated.
Saying solar PV is 'renewable' without saying it is intermittent. Give the advantage (no emissions, free fuel). Give the disadvantage too (it depends on the weather).
examTips: For 'why high voltage in the grid' questions, say two things. (1) P = IV, so high V means low I. (2) P_lost = I²R, so low I means much less power wasted. Give both equations for full marks.
Transformer equation: V₁/V₂ = n₁/n₂. Check your answer: does the voltage go up if the secondary has more turns? If not, you divided the wrong way.
For 6-mark questions evaluating energy sources, give advantages AND disadvantages for each source. Include reliability, harm to the environment and cost.
Remember: transformers need AC. Electromagnetic induction only works with a changing current. This is a common exam question.
